Cummins has shown that high-power-density spark ignition engines are possible with ethanol, but they do require additional engineering compared to a retrofit (Green Car Congress, 2014). 3.4 DIMETHYL ETHER DME is a high-cetane alternative fuel that has similar working fluid properties to propane. As such, DME is usually stored as a liquified gas at its own vapor pressure, similar to propane. DME has a high cetane number and has been shown to be a low-/no-sooting fuel; this is attractive for use in older emissions control systems and for additional optimization of exhaust gas recirculation and combustion strategies for NO control in all combustion systems. X Since DME’s working properties are so different from those of diesel fuel, the fuel injection system and the fuel storage and delivery system require significant changes that do not allow for easy backward compatibility with diesel fuel. DME’s lower energy content by volume also requires 24 larger tanks than diesel. Tanks are similar to those for used for propane, which requires a different configuration than a liquid diesel tank. 3.5 AMMONIA Anhydrous ammonia (NH ) is classified as flammable but has the lowest flame speed (7 cm/s 3 compared to 58 cm/s for gasoline or 36 cm/s for methanol) and the highest ignition energy of any alternative fuel under consideration. It also has an extremely low cetane number (very high-octane rating). Ammonia is widely used as a chemical and working fluid but has not achieved commercial success as an alternative fuel. There is active research on ammonia. Its low flame speed and high ignition energy make it problematic for use in conventional spark-ignition systems and the high octane makes it unsuitable as a drop-in compression ignition. Ammonia’s working properties are nearly identical to those of propane, which means liquid ammonia can result from compressing the gas to a few bars for storage and transportation. Ammonia has significant corrosivity challenges, as well as lubricity challenges, which require different fuel injection systems than those for other fuels that have similar working properties. Propane-like vapor compression properties also require the use of a propane-style tank. The lower energy density of ammonia requires a larger tank compared to traditional diesel. In addition, the toxicity of anhydrous ammonia requires different handling considerations than other fuels. Ammonia can be used in dual-fuel applications and work is ongoing to understand the NO and X N O tradeoffs with efficiency. 2 25 4 LEVELIZED COSTS OF LOCOMOTIVE ENERGY SYSTEMS This section evaluates the costs associated with the use of biofuels in freight rail. While RD can serve as a 100% drop-in replacement for diesel, BD blends above 25% (B25) require engine modifications or fuel additives. Section 4.1 first analyzes the fuel cost of biofuel mixes by estimating the levelized cost of operation (LCO), and Section 4.2 takes a deeper look at a case study of intermodal freight operation between Chicago and Los Angeles.
